title: REspiratory drive and effort under PROpofol and Sufentanil sedation – a pharmacodynamic response-surface modeling study
summary:
Patients in the intensive care unit are very seriously ill. As part of their treatment, they may need help with breathing using a ventilator. During the first days of this therapy, the ventilator does most of the breathing work. As patients begin to wake up, they start to take over some of the breathing effort themselves.

Breathing on their own generally has positive effects on recovery. It can improve how well the lungs are filled with air and help maintain the strength and health of the breathing muscles. However, spontaneous breathing during ventilation can also have side effects. For example, the breathing muscles may be overworked or underworked. This can weaken them and may lead to a longer time on the ventilator.

The strain on the breathing muscles can be measured. For this, we look at breathing drive (the body’s signal to breathe) and breathing effort (how hard the patient breathes). These are often reduced or changed by medications used in intensive care to relieve pain and keep patients calm. The most commonly used drugs are Propofol and Sufentanil. However, how these drugs are processed in the body and how they act can vary greatly between patients. In particular, their exact effects on breathing drive and effort are not well understood, especially when considering this variability.

Both too little and too much breathing drive or effort can harm the lungs and increase the risk of complications and death. The level of support provided by the ventilator also affects breathing drive.

To reduce side effects as much as possible, it is important to understand and control breathing drive and effort. In this study, we want to examine in more detail how sedation affects breathing drive. We also want to study the effect of ventilator support.

We will investigate the exact influence of sedation and ventilator support on breathing drive. To do this, we will measure the levels of Propofol and Sufentanil in the blood. This allows us to know exactly how much of the drugs is in the body, regardless of how they are processed or eliminated. We will then analyze how these drug levels are related to breathing drive. We will also examine their effect on breathing effort. In addition, we want to study how ventilator support and sedation interact in influencing breathing drive.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Invasively ventilated patients receiving assisted ventilation
- Sedation with propofol and sufentanil
- Admission to one of the participating intensive care units at University Hospital Erlangen: IOI 1, IOI 2, IOI 3-ICC
Exclusion criteria:
- Expected imminent death despite maximal therapy (poor prognosis)
- Pregnancy
- Patient institutionalized by judicial or administrative order
- Administration of sedative agents other than propofol and sufentanil
